Wealth redistribution: Taking from the wealthy to help everyone else is the classic left-wing idea. The parties behind it also tend to be socially liberal, so it sits low as well as far left.
Deregulating markets: Cutting red tape is a favourite of the economic right. It says little about personal freedom, so it stays close to the middle vertically.
Cutting taxes: Tax cuts are backed by the economic right, often alongside parties that favour traditional values. That pulls it a little way up the grid.
Public services first: Parties that put hospitals and schools ahead of tax cuts sit well to the left, and most are socially liberal too.
Strict immigration limits: The parties pushing hardest for limits are strongly authoritarian, but they come from both sides on the economy. So it sits high up and only slightly right.
Liberal immigration: Open-door parties lean left and are strongly liberal on personal freedom. It's one of the clearest low-and-left ideas.
Multiculturalism: Parties that welcome many cultures living side by side lean left and liberal.
Assimilation: Expecting newcomers to adopt the local culture is backed mostly by authoritarian parties, with a mild lean to the right.
Tough on crime: Harsher policing and sentences are pushed by authoritarian parties from across the economic spectrum, so it sits high and only a bit right.
Civil liberties first: Putting freedoms ahead of security is a libertarian instinct. It leans left because left-wing parties are the ones leading on it today.
LGBTQ+ rights: Backed by socially liberal parties, mostly on the centre-left, so it sits low and a little left.
Same-sex marriage: Like wider LGBTQ+ rights, this is a socially liberal idea with only a mild economic lean.
Women's rights policies: Equal pay and parental leave are championed mostly by left-leaning, socially liberal parties.
Religion in politics: Parties that want faith to shape the law are strongly traditional, so it sits near the top. It has little to say about economics.
Secular government: Keeping religion out of lawmaking is backed by liberal parties, mostly centre-left.
Nationalism: Putting the nation first is the signature of authoritarian parties, most of whom lean right on economics.
Cosmopolitanism: Seeing yourself as a citizen of the world is a liberal, left-leaning outlook.
Trade protectionism: This one splits the middle. Left parties protect jobs and nationalist right parties protect industry, so it lands near the centre line but high on the grid.
Free trade: Open borders for goods and services means fewer state controls, which makes it right-leaning and liberal.
Devolving power: Giving regions more say appeals to all kinds of parties, so it ends up close to the centre.
Strong executive: Letting leaders act without heavy constraint is authoritarian at heart, and it appeals to parties across the economic spectrum.
Limits on leaders: Checks and balances are favoured by liberal parties, more often on the left.
Government sway over judges: Wanting politicians to have a say over courts is a strongly authoritarian stance, with a mild lean right.
Independent judiciary: Almost every party says it backs independent courts, so this sits near the middle, leaning a little liberal.
Climate policy over growth: Parties willing to accept slower growth for lower emissions lean left and liberal.
Growth over environment: Putting the economy first is right-leaning. In practice the parties that do it are also traditional and authoritarian.
Ethnic minority rights: Extra protections for minorities are backed by left-leaning, socially liberal parties.
Environment over growth: Protecting nature even at some economic cost is a left and liberal position, and Green parties lead on it.
Self-reliance over welfare: Expecting people to look after themselves is the mirror image of redistribution. It sits well to the right, with a mild authoritarian tilt.
Regulated markets: Strong rules on business are a left-wing instinct, and the parties behind them are mostly socially liberal.
Centralised government: Parties that want decisions made nationally are strongly authoritarian, with little economic lean.
Direct democracy: Letting the public decide big questions by referendum is mostly a populist idea. Populists sit high on the grid but all over the economic spectrum.
Representative democracy: Leaving big decisions to elected officials is the established view, so it sits close to the centre.
Rural interests: Putting the countryside first is mostly a traditional, authoritarian position, with a small lean right.
Urban interests: Putting cities first is a liberal position, with a mild lean to the right.
Anti-establishment politics: Attacking elites is a populist theme. It sits high on the grid and close to the middle on the economy because both left and right do it.
Fighting corruption: Almost every party says it wants a cleaner politics, so this lands close to the middle.
International authority over security: Parties that want a shared foreign and defence policy lean slightly liberal, and they come from all along the economic line.
Free movement across borders: Letting goods, services and workers move freely appeals to the centre and centre-right, with a lean liberal.
Deeper international union: Pooling more power in a shared body is backed by centrist, liberal-leaning parties.
Leaving international unions: Taking powers back from shared bodies is backed by nationalist, authoritarian parties, mostly a bit right of centre.
Military strength: Parties that give the armed forces a lot of attention lean right and a little authoritarian.
Anti-militarism: Parties that stress peace and disarmament lean left and a little liberal.
Nationalisation: Putting industry in public hands is a left-wing idea. It says little about personal freedom, so it sits at the centre line.
Expanding education: Spending more on schools and universities is mildly left, and it's backed from across the spectrum.
Traditional morality: Parties that talk most about traditional values are strongly authoritarian and lean right.
Equality: Parties that talk about fairness and equal treatment lean left and liberal.
Trade unions: Backing for organised labour is a left-wing idea that sits about level on personal freedom.
Human rights and freedoms: Parties that talk most about human rights are liberal, with almost no economic lean.
Standing up to Russia: Backing sanctions and support for Ukraine cuts across the usual divides. Its supporters sit just right of centre and slightly libertarian.
Accommodating Russia: Parties that want warmer ties with Moscow are mostly authoritarian, and many of them lean left on the economy, which puts this up and to the left.
Immigration as top priority: The parties that campaign hardest on immigration are overwhelmingly authoritarian, so this sits near the top of the grid, a little right of centre.
Climate as top priority: Parties that put climate first are the Greens and their allies: clearly left and among the most libertarian on the grid.
Redistribution as top priority: Putting inequality at the centre of politics is a left-wing habit, and the parties that do it are mostly socially liberal too.
Europe as top priority: Parties that talk most about the EU come from both sides, strong supporters and strong opponents, so they average out close to the middle.
